title: Paper 1 Question 3: how the writer structures the text
specPoints: Paper 1 Section A: Question 3 (AO2, 8 marks): structure across the whole source

tips.title: The three bullets are the plan
tips.body: Beginning and what it makes the reader expect; how and why the focus changes; other structural features. Answer each in one sentence before writing, and the paragraphs are the sentences expanded.

tips.title: Seven features to know by name
tips.body: Exposition, focus shift, narrative perspective, temporal shift, flashback, dialogue, anti-climax: the June 2024 scheme's own list. Add cyclical and withholding. A feature named exactly is half the point; its effect is the other half.

tips.title: Language earns nothing here
tips.body: If a paragraph in a Question 3 answer contains the word simile, metaphor or adjective, it is answering Question 2. Question 3 is marked for structural features and their effects, and a language point, however good, is not one.

tips.title: Read the source as a journey
tips.body: Where does it start, where does it move, where does it end, and what does the reader expect at each stage? Four questions, asked during the 15 minutes of reading, give the whole answer to Question 3.

tips.title: The word reader in every sentence
tips.body: The question is how the writer structured the text to interest you as a reader. A sentence without an effect on the reader is a description of the text, not an analysis of its structure.

tips.title: Set-up and pay-off
tips.body: When a text tells you something ordinary, ask what it is for. The honey-cake paragraph in Miss Brill exists so that passing the baker's by can be felt. A set-up named with its pay-off is a paragraph-level structural point.

why.matters: Every text has a shape, and the shape does work the words alone cannot: it decides what the reader expects, what they wait for, and what they discover. Question 3 tests whether a reader can see that shape, and it is the question students most often answer wrongly, by writing about language, because language is what they have been taught to notice. Reading for structure is also the skill behind writing well: a story or a description earns its marks on Paper 1 Section B by its shape as much as its sentences, and the writer who can see how Mansfield builds a rise, a fall and a return can build one.

examples.title: Why a film starts where it starts
examples.body: A film that opens on a car chase and a film that opens on a kitchen are making the same choice Question 3 asks about: what to focus the audience on first, and what to make them expect. The cut from one place to another, the flashback, the scene in which someone else finally speaks about the main character: these are the structural features of the mark scheme, in pictures. A viewer who can say why a scene is placed where it is has learned the question.

examples.title: A speech, a story, a joke
examples.body: Anything told aloud is built: a beginning that sets up, a middle that shifts, an ending that returns or reverses. A joke is nothing but structure, a set-up and a pay-off. A best man's speech that ends by returning to something said at the start, a news report that opens on one person and widens to the whole story: the reader who can name the shape can make the shape, and the two skills are the two halves of Paper 1.

steps.title: Question 3: the whole text as a shape
steps.body:
Question 3 turns from a passage to the whole source. The wording is fixed: *You now need to think about the whole of the source. How has the writer structured the text to interest you as a reader?* Three bullets follow: what the writer focuses your attention on at the beginning; how and why the writer changes this focus as the source develops; any other structural features that interest you. Eight marks, AO2, four levels with the same names as Question 2.

**What structure means here.** The mark scheme says structural features can be at whole-text level, such as beginnings, endings and shifts of perspective; at paragraph level, such as a change of topic or how paragraphs connect; and at sentence level when a sentence contributes to the shape of the whole. A response that writes only about language is answering Question 2's objective, and earns little here however good it is.

**The habit to build.** Read the source as a journey: where it starts, where it moves, where it ends, and what the reader is made to expect, wait for, or discover along the way.

rows: Whole text
Opening; ending; a shift of perspective or time
Where does it start, move and finish?
Paragraph
A change of topic; a paragraph that answers an earlier one
What does each new paragraph do to the focus?
Sentence
A single short sentence that turns the text
Does this sentence change the shape of the whole?

check.prompt: A student answers Question 3 with three paragraphs on similes, adjectives and verbs in the source. What does the mark scheme say?
check.solution: Question 3 is marked for structural features and their effects. A language answer, however sharp, is answering a different question, and the AO2 marks for structure cannot be earned by similes. The scheme's note about language outside the given lines belongs to Questions 2 and 4; here the point is simpler: structure, not language.

options: The response is transferred to Question 2, where language is what is assessed
The response is marked as normal, because language and structure are both AO2 and count the same in the examiners' marking
It earns very little, because Question 3 assesses structure and a language answer, however good, is answering a different objective
The response earns full marks if the analysis is perceptive, whatever it is about

steps.title: The features the scheme names
steps.body:
The June 2024 indicative content for Question 3 is a list of the structural features examiners were ready to reward in that source, and it is a good list to learn.

**Exposition:** the opening establishes the setting and the character's state, so the reader knows what to watch. **Focus shifts:** the text moves from outside to inside, with the verandah as a space in between. **Narrative perspective:** third person, which allows a switch between what is described and what the characters think. **Temporal shifts:** “as time passed” and “one day” move the reader through time without much happening, and that is the point. **Flashback:** a brief glimpse of an earlier life to contrast with the present. **Dialogue:** an exchange that builds tension. **Anti-climax:** an expected argument that subsides when one character apologises.

Every one of these is a choice about order, movement or viewpoint, not about words. That is the difference between Question 3 and Question 2.

rows: Exposition
Sets what to watch and what to expect
Focus shift
Moves the eye: outside to inside, wide to close
Narrative perspective

Temporal shift

Raises an expectation and lets it drop

check.solution: A shift of focus is a choice about where the text moves; the others are choices of words. The scheme lists focus shifts among the features it rewards for Question 3, and it lists similes, verbs and adjectives under Question 2.

A verb chosen for its violence, such as beat, which makes the heat feel like an attack on the character

steps.title: Miss Brill as a whole: where it goes
steps.body:
The previous topic printed the opening of *Miss Brill*. Here is the shape of the whole story, and then its ending, so that the structure can be read end to end.

**The movement.** The story opens on the sky and the fur, then widens to the band and the crowd. Miss Brill watches, listening in on other people. Then a discovery: “It was like a play. It was exactly like a play.” She realises that “They were all on the stage.” and that “Even she had a part and came every Sunday.” The band plays, her eyes fill with tears, and she feels the whole company about to sing. Then a young couple sit down where an old couple had been, and she overhears what they say about her. And then this:

> On her way home she usually bought a slice of honey-cake at the baker's. It was her Sunday treat. Sometimes there was an almond in her slice, sometimes not. It made a great difference. If there was an almond it was like carrying home a tiny present—a surprise—something that might very well not have been there. She hurried on the almond Sundays and struck the match for the kettle in quite a dashing way.

> But to-day she passed the baker's by, climbed the stairs, went into the little dark room—her room like a cupboard—and sat down on the red eiderdown. She sat there for a long time. The box that the fur came out of was on the bed. She unclasped the necklet quickly; quickly, without looking, laid it inside. But when she put the lid on she thought she heard something crying.

**The shape.** Out of the box and into the park; a widening of attention to the whole crowd; a rising idea that she belongs to it; a fall, delivered in someone else's voice; and back into the room, into the box. The ending answers the opening.

nodes.text: The fur out of its box
The fur back in its box

visuals.alt: A flow chart of the structure of Miss Brill from the fur coming out of its box, through the park and the idea of the play, to the young couple and the fur going back into the box

check.prompt: How does the ending of Miss Brill relate to its opening?
check.solution: The opening rubs life back into the fur's dim eyes; the ending puts the fur back in its box and hears something crying. A structure that returns to its beginning, changed, is called cyclical, and here the return carries the meaning: what happened to her has happened to the fur.

markScheme.description: It answers it: the fur that came out of its box, with life rubbed back into its eyes, goes back into the box, and something cries

options: It answers it: the fur that came out of its box, with life rubbed back into its eyes, goes back into the box, and something cries
It ignores it: the ending is about the honey-cake and has nothing to do with the fur
It repeats it: the story ends with the same description of the sky, the light and the gardens with which it began, repeated word for word
It contradicts it: the fur is thrown away at the end after being treasured at the beginning

steps.title: Beginnings: what the writer puts first, and why
steps.body:
The first bullet under Question 3 asks what the writer focuses your attention on at the beginning. The answer is never just *the weather*; it is what the choice of first thing does.

*Miss Brill* begins with the sky, “the blue sky powdered with gold”, and only then with the fur and the woman. The effect is to place the reader outside, in the bright afternoon, before letting them in to her; the story is going to be about a woman who lives by looking outward, and the first sentence looks outward with her.

The June 2024 source did the opposite. It began “suddenly, the heat became intolerable”, which the scheme's Level 4 example read as exposition that puts the character already at breaking point, so that the reader expects a moment when she snaps. A beginning sets up an expectation, and the rest of the text either pays it or withholds it.

**Write it as a choice.** *The writer opens with … so that the reader …* and then say what the opening leads the reader to expect.

rows: Miss Brill
The sky and the light, then the fur, then her
A story seen through her outward-looking eyes
The June 2024 source
The heat, suddenly intolerable
A breaking point
props.title: Two openings

visuals.alt: A table comparing the openings of Miss Brill and the June 2024 source: what each focuses on and what it leads the reader to expect

check.prompt: Why does it matter that Miss Brill opens with the sky and the gardens before the woman?
check.solution: The order is the choice. Beginning outside and moving in mirrors a woman who lives by watching; a story that opened on her room would set up a different expectation. Saying what the beginning leads the reader to expect is the point of the first bullet.

markScheme.description: It places the reader outside, looking, before letting them in to her, which is how she herself lives

options: It delays the introduction of the character because the writer wanted a slow start
It places the reader outside, looking, before letting them in to her, which is how she herself lives
It shows that the story is really about the gardens and the band rather than about her
It tells the reader the weather, which is needed to understand why she is wearing a fur on a fine day and why she notices the chill

steps.title: A Level 4 paragraph on the ending
steps.body: The ending is where the structure of Miss Brill pays off, and a paragraph on it can carry two of the three bullets at once.

visuals.problem: Write a paragraph on how the ending of Miss Brill is structured to affect the reader.

steps.text: Name the shift: the story moves from the crowded park to “her room like a cupboard”, a change of place that is also a change of scale, from a whole company to one woman alone.
steps.note: A focus shift, named, with its effect.

steps.text: Name the withholding: the paragraph before tells the reader about the honey-cake she usually buys; the next begins “But to-day she passed the baker's by”. A habit is set up so that its breaking can be felt.
steps.note: A structural feature at paragraph level: one paragraph exists to make the next one hurt.

steps.text: Name the return: the fur went into the box and, when the lid goes on, “she thought she heard something crying”. The reader remembers the eyes at the start asking “What has been happening to me?”
steps.note: The ending answers the opening; the reader supplies the meaning.

steps.text: Name the perspective: the crying is heard, not explained, because the narration stays inside her and she will not say the thing about herself.
steps.note: Third person close to her: the reader knows what she does not say.

steps.text: Say what it does to the reader: the story never states that she has been humiliated, and the structure makes the reader feel it instead.
steps.note: Effect on the reader, which is what the question asks for.

visuals.alt: Four boxes on the structure of the ending of Miss Brill: the shift of place, the withheld cake, the return to the box and the perspective that hears rather than explains

check.prompt: What does the paragraph about the honey-cake do for the structure of the ending?
check.solution: The paragraph exists for the sake of the one after it: a habit is established so that its breaking registers. That is structure at paragraph level, and naming what the set-up does for the reader is the analysis the top level rewards.

markScheme.description: It sets up a habit so that the next paragraph, in which she passes the baker's by, can be felt as a loss without being explained

options: It gives the reader a break from the sad mood of the scene in the park by describing something pleasant that she enjoys every week
It shows that Miss Brill is poor, because she can only afford a slice of cake once a week
It sets up a habit so that the next paragraph, in which she passes the baker's by, can be felt as a loss without being explained
It introduces a new character, the baker, who will be important at the end of the story

steps.title: Shifts: focus, time, place and voice
steps.body:
The second bullet asks how and why the focus changes as the source develops. Four kinds of shift cover most texts.

**Focus:** wide to close or close to wide. Miss Brill's attention widens from the fur to the crowd and narrows again to the one couple on her bench.

**Time:** a jump forward, a return to the past, a slowing down. The June 2024 source moved through time with “as time passed”; Miss Brill's ending jumps to the walk home and then to the room.

**Place:** the park to the room, the cupboard-sized room after the whole company.

**Voice:** whose words the reader is given. For most of the story the reader has Miss Brill's thoughts. Then, for a few lines, the young couple speak, and the shift to their voices is the story's blow: the reader hears her described from outside for the only time.

**Always say why.** A shift is not a point until its effect is named: what the reader now sees, expects or understands that they did not before.

rows: Focus
Fur, then crowd, then one couple
Widens her world, then narrows it to the people who will break it
Time
The afternoon, then the walk home, then the room
Moves the reader from the event to its consequence
Place
Park to a room like a cupboard
Scale collapses with her
Voice
Her thoughts, then the couple's words
She is seen from outside for the only time

check.prompt: Why is the shift to the young couple's dialogue the structural centre of the story?
check.solution: The story has stayed inside her thoughts; the couple's words are the first view of her from outside, and they answer the idea of the play with cruelty. Naming the shift of voice and what it does to the reader is a Level 4 structural point.

markScheme.description: For the only time the reader hears Miss Brill described from outside, and her idea of belonging to the performance is broken in someone else's voice

options: Because the couple are the main characters and the story has been waiting for them to arrive
Because the young couple explain to the reader what the story has been about
Because dialogue is more interesting to read than description, and the story, which has been description and thought for several pages, needed some variety at that point
For the only time the reader hears Miss Brill described from outside, and her idea of belonging to the performance is broken in someone else's voice

steps.title: Map the whole text
steps.body:
Take the three bullets and answer each for Miss Brill in one sentence, before writing anything longer.

1. What does the writer focus the reader's attention on at the beginning, and what does that lead the reader to expect?
2. How and why does the focus change: name two shifts and what each does.
3. What other structural feature interests you: the withheld cake, the return to the box, the dialogue, the single sentence at the end?

Then check every sentence for the word *reader*. If it is missing, the effect is missing.

check.solution: The first bullet wants what the writer focuses on first and what that does to the reader's expectations. The sentence about looking outward names the focus and the expectation. Summarising the story, listing language features, or naming the setting answers something else.

steps.title: Interest: the word in the question
steps.body:
The question asks how the writer structured the text *to interest you as a reader*, and the top level asks for analysis of the effects of structural choices. Every point therefore ends on the reader: what they are made to expect, wait for, notice or feel.

**Four effects that structure produces.** *Expectation*: an opening that promises a breaking point. *Tension*: dialogue that tightens; a habit set up so it can be broken. *Surprise or reversal*: a voice from outside; an anti-climax where an argument was expected. *Recognition*: an ending that returns to the beginning so the reader sees what has changed.

**Judicious examples.** Two or three features that show the shape of the whole beat a list of every paragraph break. The June 2024 Level 4 example took the opening and one time shift and read them together as a woman losing her grip on time.

**Terminology that names structure.** Exposition, focus, perspective, temporal shift, flashback, cyclical, withholding, anti-climax. *Simile* and *adjective* belong to Question 2; used here they signal that the question has been misread.

boxes.title: Tension
boxes.body: What is tightened or set up to break

boxes.title: Reversal
boxes.body: A voice from outside; an anti-climax

visuals.alt: Four boxes on the effects structure produces in a reader: expectation, tension, reversal and recognition

check.prompt: Which sentence about Miss Brill would the scheme place at Level 4 for Question 3?
check.solution: The sentence about the return to the box names a structural choice, the cyclical ending, and says what it makes the reader do. The sentence about beginning, middle and end is empty; the simile is a language point; the last is a summary of what happens with a feeling attached.

markScheme.description: By returning at the end to the fur that came out of its box in the first paragraph, the writer makes the reader recognise in the crying of the fur what Miss Brill will not say about herself

options: The story has a beginning, a middle and an end, and the writer uses paragraphs to separate the different parts of the afternoon from each other, which helps the reader to follow the order of events and to see where one part stops and the next begins
By returning at the end to the fur that came out of its box in the first paragraph, the writer makes the reader recognise in the crying of the fur what Miss Brill will not say about herself
The writer uses the simile of the fur being like a little rogue biting its tail, which makes the reader picture the fur as a lively animal
The ending is sad because Miss Brill goes home without her cake and puts the fur away, which shows that the young couple have upset her

steps.title: Question 3 in one page
steps.body:
Structure is the shape of the whole text, and Question 3 pays eight marks for reading it.

- **The question is fixed:** how has the writer structured the text to interest you as a reader; three bullets: the beginning, the changes of focus, other features.
- **Three levels:** whole text (openings, endings, shifts of perspective or time), paragraph (topic changes, a paragraph that sets up the next), sentence (one that turns the whole).
- **The scheme's features:** exposition, focus shifts, narrative perspective, temporal shifts, flashback, dialogue, anti-climax.
- **Every point ends on the reader:** expectation, tension, reversal, recognition.
- **Language only earns little.** Similes belong to Question 2.
- **Miss Brill's shape:** out of the box and into the park; widening to the crowd; the idea of the play; the couple's voices; back to the room and the box.

Read every source as a journey before answering anything about it.

rows: Beginning
Sky and light, then the fur, then her
Looking outward with her; expecting a story of watching
Change
Widening to the crowd; the play; the couple's voices
Belonging built, then broken from outside
Other features
The cake set up and passed by; the fur back in its box
A loss felt, not explained; recognition

visuals.alt: A summary table of the three bullets of Question 3 answered for Miss Brill, each with its effect on the reader

check.prompt: Complete the name of the structure in which a text ends by returning to its beginning, changed: a ... structure.
check.solution: Cyclical, or circular: the ending returns to the opening. In Miss Brill the fur comes out of its box in the first paragraph and goes back into it in the last, and the return carries what the story never states.

markScheme.description: cyclical

questions.prompt: How many marks is Question 3 worth?
questions.solution: Question 3 is worth 8 marks, the same as Question 2, and it is marked in the same four levels. The difference is the object: the whole text and its shape, rather than the language of a passage.

questions.prompt: Which part of the source does Question 3 cover?
questions.solution: Question 3 begins *You now need to think about the whole of the source*. Question 2 gives a passage, Question 4 gives a part; Question 3 is the only reading question about the shape of everything.

markScheme.description: The whole of the source, from the first line to the last

options: The whole of the source, from the first line to the last
The first paragraph only, where the exposition is
The lines the question prints, as in Question 2
The second half of the source, from a stated line to the end

questions.prompt: What is the term for the part of a story's opening that establishes the setting and situation?
questions.solution: Exposition: the establishing of setting, character and situation. The June 2024 scheme used the word for the opening of its source, where the character is already at breaking point with the heat, so that the reader expects her to snap.

markScheme.description: exposition

questions.prompt: What are the three bullets printed under Question 3?
questions.solution: The three bullets are the beginning, the changes of focus, and other structural features. The bullets about words and sentence forms belong to Question 2.

markScheme.description: What the writer focuses your attention on at the beginning; how and why the focus changes as the source develops; any other structural features that interest you

options: Words and phrases; language features and techniques; sentence forms, and the effect of each on the reader of the given passage
What the writer focuses your attention on at the beginning; how and why the focus changes as the source develops; any other structural features that interest you
The characters and how they are introduced; the setting and how it is described; the atmosphere and how it changes
The beginning and what it establishes; the climax and how it is reached; the resolution and what it settles

questions.prompt: Which of these is a temporal shift?
questions.solution: A temporal shift moves the reader through time. The June 2024 scheme listed the source's *as time passed* and *one day* as temporal shifts that let time pass without much happening. The move from outside to inside is a focus shift, and the comparison is a simile.

markScheme.description: A phrase such as as time passed or one day, which moves the reader forward in time

options: A move from describing the outside of a house to describing the inside of it in detail
A change from the narrator's description to a character's thoughts
A phrase such as as time passed or one day, which moves the reader forward in time
A comparison of one thing with another using like or as

questions.prompt: What is an anti-climax, as the June 2024 scheme used the word?
questions.solution: The scheme described the source's anti-climax as the expectation of an argument that subsides when the husband apologises. Structure can build tension and then release it; naming the release and its effect is a structural point.

markScheme.description: An expectation that is raised and then allowed to drop, such as an argument that subsides when a character apologises

options: The most exciting moment of a story, where the tension is highest and the reader most wants to know what happens next
An ending in which everything that has happened is explained to the reader so that no question is left open
A moment of dialogue in which two characters disagree and neither of them will give way to the other
An expectation that is raised and then allowed to drop, such as an argument that subsides when a character apologises

questions.prompt: Why does the narrative perspective of Miss Brill matter to its structure?
questions.solution: The narration is third person but stays close to her, giving the reader her thoughts. That is what makes the shift to the couple's voices structural: for a few lines the reader is outside her, and the story turns there.

markScheme.description: The reader stays inside her thoughts until the couple speak, so their words are the only view of her from outside and land as a blow

options: The reader stays inside her thoughts until the couple speak, so their words are the only view of her from outside and land as a blow
The story is told in the first person, so the reader only knows what Miss Brill chooses to tell them about herself and about the afternoon in the park
The narrator is a young person in the park, which explains why the couple are treated sympathetically
The perspective changes in every paragraph, so the reader sees the park from many points of view

questions.prompt: Put the five stages of Miss Brill in the order the story presents them.
questions.solution: Out of the box; the widening; the idea of the play; the couple; back into the box. The order is the structure: a rise to belonging, a fall delivered from outside, and a return to the opening, changed.

markScheme.description: the five stages in order

items: The fur comes out of its box and Miss Brill goes to the park
Her attention widens to the band, the crowd and other people's lives
She realises that it is like a play and that she has a part in it
The young couple sit down and she overhears what they say about her
She goes home without her cake and puts the fur back in its box

questions.prompt: What does Miss Brill hear as she puts the lid on the box at the end of the story?
questions.solution: She thought she heard something crying. The story never says who; the structure has already told the reader, because the fur came out of the box in the first paragraph with its eyes asking what had been happening to it.

markScheme.description: something crying

questions.prompt: A student writes: the writer uses short sentences at the end of Miss Brill. Why is this not yet a Question 3 point?
questions.solution: The scheme allows sentence-level features when they contribute to whole-text structure. The short final sentence closes the story on the crying, and saying what that closing does to the reader turns a sentence-level observation into a structural point.

markScheme.description: It names a feature without saying what it does to the shape of the whole or to the reader; a sentence-level point counts for structure only when its effect on the whole is explained

options: It is about sentences, and the mark scheme says in plain words that sentences never count as structure under any circumstances, since only paragraphs and whole texts can have a structure
It names a feature without saying what it does to the shape of the whole or to the reader; a sentence-level point counts for structure only when its effect on the whole is explained
It is wrong, because the sentences at the end of Miss Brill are all long and winding, like the sentence that opens the story on the sky and the light
It should be in Question 2, and any comment on sentences made in Question 3 is deducted from the marks awarded for Question 3

questions.prompt: Which of these best explains why the June 2024 Level 4 example read the opening and a time shift together?
questions.solution: The Level 4 example connected the exposition, a character at breaking point, with a time shift that suggested time had become immeasurable to her: one shape, built across the text. Judicious examples are ones that connect; the number is not prescribed.

markScheme.description: Because reading two features as one shape, a woman already at breaking point and time losing its measure for her, shows how the structure builds an effect across the text

options: Because the mark scheme requires exactly two features to be discussed in every Level 4 answer, no more and no fewer, and the example shows the two the examiners preferred
Because the opening and the time shift are the only structural features in that source, so there was nothing else for the example to discuss
Because reading two features as one shape, a woman already at breaking point and time losing its measure for her, shows how the structure builds an effect across the text
Because the examiners prefer answers that begin at the start of the text and work through it in order, and an example must show the preferred order

questions.prompt: In Miss Brill, what is the structural function of the paragraph about the old invalid gentleman to whom she reads the newspaper?
questions.solution: The paragraph steps out of the park and into her working week, and it does so at the height of the play idea: she imagines telling the old man that she is an actress. A flashback placed there shows the idea spreading through her whole life, which makes its collapse a few paragraphs later the larger.

markScheme.description: It is a brief flashback inside the play idea, so that her new sense of herself as an actress reaches back into the rest of her week and shows how much the idea means to her

options: It introduces a new plot in which the old gentleman will become important later in the story, when he wakes and discovers that his reader has been an actress all along
It shows that Miss Brill has a job, which explains how she can afford a fur and a slice of cake every Sunday, and tells the reader that she is not as poor as her room suggests
It is a digression that the writer should have cut, since it interrupts the scene in the park at the moment when the reader most wants to stay there
It is a brief flashback inside the play idea, so that her new sense of herself as an actress reaches back into the rest of her week and shows how much the idea means to her

questions.prompt: The mark scheme's Level 4 descriptor for Question 3 asks for a range of examples chosen with judgement. What single word does it use?
questions.solution: Judicious: selects a range of judicious examples. As in Question 2, it means chosen for the question and for how they connect, not every paragraph break in the text.

markScheme.description: judicious

questions.prompt: A paragraph on the ending of Miss Brill is built from these sentences. Put them in the order that moves from the feature to the reader.
questions.solution: Feature, then what the feature is, then what the reader experiences, then the effect. The reader arrives before the final sentence names the effect, because the effect is built out of what the reader has been made to feel.

markScheme.description: the four sentences in order

items: The story shifts from the park to her room, described as like a cupboard
The change of place is also a change of scale, from a whole company of people to one woman alone
The reader, who has shared her sense of belonging to the performance, is shut in with her
The effect is that the humiliation is felt through the structure before it is ever named

questions.prompt: Write one Level 4 paragraph on how the writer structures the ending of Miss Brill to interest the reader. Use at least two structural features, name each, and end each point on what it does to the reader.
questions.solution: Mansfield structures the ending as a series of returns and withholdings that let the reader feel what Miss Brill will not say. The first move is a shift of place and scale: from the park, where she has just imagined the whole company about to sing, to “her room like a cupboard”, so that the reader who shared her sense of belonging to a performance is shut in with her alone. The second is a set-up made only to be broken: a paragraph tells the reader that on her way home she usually buys a slice of honey-cake and that an almond in it makes a great difference, and the next begins “But to-day she passed the baker's by”, so that a small habit, established in three sentences, becomes the measure of the afternoon's damage. The third is the return: the fur that came out of its box in the first paragraph, its dim eyes asking “What has been happening to me?”, goes back into the box, and when the lid goes on “she thought she heard something crying”. The narration stays inside her to the last word, hearing rather than explaining, so the reader is left to supply what has happened, and does. The features work as one shape: the story returns to where it began, changed, and the reader recognises in the crying of the fur the thing the story has never stated.

markScheme.description: two features named
effects on the reader
checked details
read as one shape

criteria.text: Names at least two structural features of the ending precisely: the shift of place and scale, the set-up and withholding of the cake, the return to the box, the perspective that hears rather than explains

questions.prompt: How has the writer structured Miss Brill to interest you as a reader? Write a full Question 3 answer of the length you would write in the exam, using the three bullets: what the writer focuses on at the beginning, how and why the focus changes, and any other structural features.
questions.solution: Mansfield begins by focusing the reader's attention outward, on “the blue sky powdered with gold” and the gardens, before the fur and the woman appear, so that the reader starts by looking as Miss Brill looks and expects a story of watching rather than of doing. The focus then widens, from the fur to the band and the crowd and to other people's conversations, and the widening builds her world: the reader is given her thoughts in a close third person and shares her pleasure in it. The turning point is a shift within that world: the discovery that “It was exactly like a play.” and that she has a part in it, which the writer extends with a brief flashback to the old invalid gentleman she reads to, so that the idea reaches into the rest of her week and the reader sees how much it means. The next shift is of voice. For the only time, the young couple speak, and the reader hears Miss Brill described from outside; the belonging that the structure has built is broken in a few lines of someone else's dialogue, which is why the blow lands. The final shifts are of time and place: the walk home, the honey-cake set up in one paragraph and withheld in the next, and then “her room like a cupboard”, where the scale collapses from a whole company to one woman. The ending is cyclical. The fur that came out of its box at the start goes back into it, and the final sentence hears “something crying”, so that the reader recognises what has happened to her in what she will not say about herself.

markScheme.description: the beginning and its expectation

questions.prompt: A student begins a Question 3 answer: the writer uses the simile of light like white wine to make the opening vivid. What has gone wrong?
questions.solution: The simile is a language choice, and Question 3 asks about structure. The first bullet is about what the writer focuses on first and what that does, which is a point about order and expectation, not about the image. Starting on language is the commonest way to lose this question, because the marks are for structural features and their effects.

markScheme.description: The answer has started with a language point, and an answer that stays on language earns little on a question marked for structure

options: The answer has started with a language point, and an answer that stays on language earns little on a question marked for structure
Nothing: the simile is in the opening, and the first bullet is about the opening
The simile has been misidentified, since it is a metaphor
The student should have started with the ending, since Question 3 is marked from the end of the text backwards, so that the last paragraph is the first thing the examiner expects to read about

questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Miss Brill has no real structure, because nothing happens: a woman goes to the park and comes home.' What is the better reading?
questions.solution: A text in which little happens can be tightly built. Miss Brill rises to the idea of the play, falls in the couple's voices, and returns to the box; the shape does what the plot does not. An answer that sees the shape as the story reads structure as the top level asks.

markScheme.description: The structure is the story: a rise to belonging built by a widening focus and the idea of the play, a fall delivered in a change of voice, and a return to the opening that carries the meaning nothing states

options: The structure is simply chronological, and an answer should list the events of the afternoon in order from the fur coming out of its box to the fur going back into it, with a comment on each

The structure is the story: a rise to belonging built by a widening focus and the idea of the play, a fall delivered in a change of voice, and a return to the opening that carries the meaning nothing states
The story has a twist ending, in which the young couple insult her, and that twist is its only structural feature worth writing about

The student is right, and the answer should say that the writer relies on language rather than structure, and then spend the rest of the answer on the language of the story instead, since that is where the marks are

examTechnique.body:
**Structure, not language.** Question 3 asks how the writer structured the whole text. A language answer earns little, however good, because the marks are for structural features and their effects.

**Use the three bullets.** Beginning and expectation; the shifts and why; other features. One sentence each during the reading time, then expand.

**Name the feature and its effect.** Exposition, focus shift, perspective, temporal shift, flashback, dialogue, anti-climax, cyclical return, withholding: each followed by what it makes the reader expect, feel or recognise.

**Judicious, not exhaustive.** Two or three features read together as one shape earn more than a list of every paragraph change. The June 2024 Level 4 example joined the opening to one time shift.

**About ten minutes.** Eight marks, the same as Question 2, and Question 4's twenty marks are still to come.
examinerErrors: Writing about similes, adjectives and verbs, which answers Question 2 and earns little on a question about structure.
Retelling the text in order and calling the retelling structure.
Naming a feature, such as a flashback, without saying what it does to the reader.
Ignoring the first bullet, so the opening and what it sets up are never discussed.
Listing every paragraph change instead of choosing the shifts that show the shape of the whole.
Leaving the ending out, when the ending is where structure most often pays off.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer reads the source as a journey and says where it starts, where it moves and where it ends, with a reason for each. It names two or three structural features exactly, the opening's exposition and what it promises, a shift of focus, time, place or voice and why it is made, a set-up and its pay-off or a return to the beginning, and ends every point on the reader: what they expect, what tightens, what reverses, what they recognise. It reads the features together as one shape rather than as a list, uses the vocabulary of structure and none of the vocabulary of language, and keeps to about ten minutes.
